title: Parshall Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Parshall wells have a 120 ft median depth, 6.2 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $13,800-$24,000.
h1: What Parshall Well Records Mean for a Rural Property
intro_html:
Buying land near Parshall means looking closely at the local well record, not relying on a countywide average. Within 5 miles of Parshall, Colorado, DWR records include 244 permitted wells, with 141 listed as constructed. The records point to relatively shallow wells on average, but fractured mountain bedrock can produce very different results from lot to lot.

The median reported depth is 120 feet and the median reported yield is 6.2 gallons per minute. Those figures are useful for planning, but they do not guarantee what a new well will find. Before buying, compare nearby well construction, yield, water level, permit type, and the proposed homesite.

sections.heading: Parshall well depth varies with the bedrock
sections.html:
Reported well depths near Parshall have a median of 120 feet. The middle half runs from 50 to 260 feet, so a driller bidding a new well should allow for a broad range rather than treating 120 feet as a target depth. The 90th-percentile depth is 400 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 1,001 feet.

About 44% of the wells are under 100 feet, while 33% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 20% are between 300 and 600 feet, with 4% at 600 feet or deeper. Nearly all permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, which is consistent with the local granite and gneiss setting. Fractured rock can change quickly across short distances.

sections.heading: Most Parshall wells produce useful household flow
sections.html:
Among the 40 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 6.2 gallons per minute. The middle half reports 3.9 to 10.0 gallons per minute. About 65% produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 25% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. About 8% report more than 15 gallons per minute and 2% report under 1 gallon per minute.

That distribution is generally workable for a household, but the low-yield records matter when evaluating a property. A well that pumps slowly may still function with storage, while a very weak well can affect occupancy and lender decisions. Ask for the well construction and pump test, not just a verbal claim about water production. An exempt household-use well is subject to Colorado rules, including the 35 gpm pumping limit.

sections.heading: Water levels are commonly shallow in Parshall
sections.html:
Only 13 records report a static water level, so the local water-level sample is limited. Within that sample, the median depth to water is 40 feet, and the middle half ranges from 7 to 50 feet. That suggests water is often encountered relatively close to the surface in reported wells, but it is not enough information to establish a long-term trend for the entire Parshall area.

The permit counts by decade also do not show a water-table trend. They describe when permits were issued, not how water levels changed. Have a driller measure the existing well’s static level after it has recovered, and compare that measurement with the well report. Seasonal conditions, pumping, fractures, and local topography can all affect the reading.

sections.heading: Parshall’s permit history shows long-term rural use
sections.html:
DWR records show permitted wells near Parshall from the 1960s through the 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2025. The records list 3 permits in the 1960s, 28 in the 1970s, 32 in the 1980s, 46 in the 1990s, 43 in the 2000s, 21 in the 2010s, and 20 in the 2020s.

Domestic and household use accounts for 78% of the permits. Stock use accounts for 13%, monitoring for 10%, and irrigation for 1%. Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, Shelton, Joe Wayne is the most active driller in these records with 17 wells, followed by Mcpherson Drilling Company, Mcpherson, Benny Don with 15, and J & J Drilling Inc., Dale, John U with 9. These names identify local record history, not a guarantee of current availability or performance.

sections.heading: A Parshall well budget starts with depth and rock
sections.html:
For fractured mountain bedrock, the drilling model uses a rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the 120-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at about $7,800 to $12,000. A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $13,800 to $24,000.

Those figures are planning estimates, not a firm bid. A deeper hole, difficult access, casing or grout requirements, hard excavation, or a poor-producing fracture can change the total. Ask each driller what is included, how standby or extra footage is billed, and whether the quote covers testing and the final connection to the home. A budget based only on the drilled hole leaves out important site costs.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic space, and dry-hole exposure
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information near Parshall includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 161 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped features do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to test the water and understand the property’s location relative to potential sources.

Low yield and dry-hole risk remain important because fractured granite and gneiss do not distribute water evenly. Review neighboring well depths, yields, and water levels before committing to a homesite. Also confirm that the lot has room for a compliant septic system, reserve area, access for drilling equipment, and utility trenching. A well permit does not by itself solve septic, building, access, or water-quality requirements.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Parshall, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Parshall is 120 feet. The middle half ranges from 50 to 260 feet, but the local record includes wells as deep as 1,001 feet. About 44% are under 100 feet and 33% are between 100 and 300 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock makes the depth on a specific lot unpredictable.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Parshall?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured granite and gneiss. At the 120-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $7,800 to $12,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $13,800 to $24,000. A driller should price access and extra footage separately.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Parshall?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 6.2 gallons per minute, based on 40 wells with yield data. The middle half ranges from 3.9 to 10.0 gallons per minute. About 65% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, but 25% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. Check the individual well test before buying.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Parshall?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that every well is safe to drink. Nearby mapped information includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 161 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well for relevant contaminants, use a qualified laboratory, and review the results before relying on the water for household use.

faq.q: Are there dry wells near Parshall, Colorado?
faq.a: The records show a fractured-bedrock setting, where water production can vary sharply between nearby properties. The data include 2% of reported yields under 1 gallon per minute, but yield information is available for only 40 wells. Review neighboring well reports, obtain a site-specific drilling opinion, and keep a contingency for extra footage or limited production.
